question: What is the primary difference between image annotation and video annotation?
options: Video annotation only uses bounding boxes
Video annotation must account for temporal consistency across frames
Image annotation requires more compute power
There is no meaningful difference
answer: Video annotation must account for temporal consistency across frames

question: What does 'frame rate' refer to in the context of video annotation?
options: The speed at which annotators must work
The number of individual frames displayed per second of video
The resolution of the video
The number of objects annotated per frame
answer: The number of individual frames displayed per second of video

question: Why might a client ask annotators to label only every 5th frame instead of every frame?
options: To make the task harder
To reduce annotation cost and time while still capturing sufficient motion data
Because labeling every frame is technically impossible
Because the model cannot process video
answer: To reduce annotation cost and time while still capturing sufficient motion data

question: What is 'interpolation' in video annotation tools used for?
options: Automatically generating annotations for frames between two manually labeled keyframes
Deleting duplicate annotations
Converting video to audio
Compressing the video file
answer: Automatically generating annotations for frames between two manually labeled keyframes

question: A 'keyframe' in video annotation is best described as:
options: Any random frame in the video
A frame where an annotator manually sets or adjusts an annotation, used as an anchor for interpolation
The first frame of the video only
A frame with no objects present
answer: A frame where an annotator manually sets or adjusts an annotation, used as an anchor for interpolation

question: Which of the following is a common video annotation task?
options: Object tracking across frames
Compiling source code
Rendering 3D models
Formatting spreadsheets
answer: Object tracking across frames

question: What is 'occlusion' in the context of video annotation?
options: When an object is partially or fully blocked from view by another object
When the video resolution is too low
When two annotators disagree
When the video file is corrupted
answer: When an object is partially or fully blocked from view by another object

question: How should an annotator typically handle an object that becomes occluded and then reappears?
options: Stop tracking it entirely and never label it again
Mark it as occluded during the occlusion period and re-associate the same track ID when it reappears
Create a brand new track ID when it reappears
Delete all previous annotations of that object
answer: Mark it as occluded during the occlusion period and re-associate the same track ID when it reappears

question: What is a 'track ID' used for in video annotation?
options: To uniquely identify the same object as it appears across multiple frames
To label the video file itself
To indicate annotator performance
To mark the video's copyright status
answer: To uniquely identify the same object as it appears across multiple frames

question: In video annotation, what does 'temporal annotation' typically refer to?
options: Labeling the start and end times of an event or action within a video
Labeling only the color of objects
Removing audio from the video
Adjusting the video's brightness
answer: Labeling the start and end times of an event or action within a video

question: Which task type would require annotators to draw a box around a person and follow them frame by frame?
options: Sentiment analysis
Multi-object tracking
Text transcription
Audio labeling
answer: Multi-object tracking

question: What is the purpose of a 'null' or 'not applicable' label option in a video annotation task?
options: To allow annotators to skip frames where the target concept is not present or not visible
To indicate the annotator is done for the day
To flag technical bugs only
It has no real purpose
answer: To allow annotators to skip frames where the target concept is not present or not visible

question: Why is consistent annotation of object boundaries important in video tasks?
options: It has no impact on downstream model performance
Inconsistent boundaries introduce noise that can degrade the accuracy of models trained on the data
It only matters for image tasks, not video
Boundaries are drawn automatically by the software regardless of annotator input
answer: Inconsistent boundaries introduce noise that can degrade the accuracy of models trained on the data

question: What does 're-identification' (Re-ID) mean in video annotation?
options: Recognizing that an object seen earlier in the video is the same object seen later, even after leaving and re-entering the frame
Renaming a video file
Identifying the annotator who labeled a clip
Resetting all annotations to default
answer: Recognizing that an object seen earlier in the video is the same object seen later, even after leaving and re-entering the frame

question: Which of these is NOT typically a video annotation output format?
options: COCO JSON
MP3 audio waveform
YOLO text format
XML (Pascal VOC style)
answer: MP3 audio waveform

question: What should an annotator do if the task guidelines are ambiguous about how to handle a specific edge case?
options: Guess and move on without documentation
Flag the case, document it, and seek clarification from the team lead or guidelines
Skip the entire video
Make up a new rule and apply it silently
answer: Flag the case, document it, and seek clarification from the team lead or guidelines

question: What is 'ground truth' data in the context of AI training?
options: Data that has been verified as accurate and is used as the standard for evaluating model or annotator performance
Raw, unlabeled video footage
Data generated entirely by an AI model
Corrupted or low-quality data
answer: Data that has been verified as accurate and is used as the standard for evaluating model or annotator performance

question: Why might video annotation tasks include audio transcription components?
options: Because multimodal models often need synchronized text, audio, and visual labels
Audio is always irrelevant to video tasks
To slow down the annotation process intentionally
Because video files never contain audio
answer: Because multimodal models often need synchronized text, audio, and visual labels

question: What is the main goal of a 'gold standard' or 'honeypot' task inserted into an annotation batch?
options: To secretly test and monitor annotator accuracy using a known-correct answer
To reward the fastest annotator
To replace the need for guidelines
To generate revenue directly
answer: To secretly test and monitor annotator accuracy using a known-correct answer

question: If an annotation platform crashes mid-task and loses your progress, what is the best first action?
options: Immediately close the platform and give up
Report the issue to support/QA and check if autosave preserved any progress before redoing the work
Falsify the missing annotations from memory without checking
Blame the previous annotator
answer: Report the issue to support/QA and check if autosave preserved any progress before redoing the work

question: What is the correct way to draw a bounding box around an object?
options: As loosely as possible to save time
Tightly fitted to the visible extent of the object with minimal background included
Always as a perfect square regardless of object shape
Covering the entire frame
answer: Tightly fitted to the visible extent of the object with minimal background included

question: What does IoU (Intersection over Union) measure?
options: The color similarity between two objects
The overlap between a predicted bounding box and the ground truth box, relative to their union
The number of objects in a frame
The speed of annotation
answer: The overlap between a predicted bounding box and the ground truth box, relative to their union

question: An IoU threshold of 0.5 is commonly used to determine what?
options: Whether a predicted detection counts as a correct match to ground truth
The video's frame rate
The annotator's pay rate
The compression ratio of the video
answer: Whether a predicted detection counts as a correct match to ground truth

question: If an object is 90% occluded but a small visible part remains, what is generally the best practice?
options: Never annotate it
Follow the specific guideline; commonly, annotate the visible portion and mark it as heavily occluded
Draw a box around the entire frame
Always skip occluded objects with no exceptions
answer: Follow the specific guideline; commonly, annotate the visible portion and mark it as heavily occluded

question: What is 'class imbalance' in an object detection dataset?
options: When some object categories appear far more frequently than others, potentially biasing the model
When bounding boxes are of different sizes
When annotators work different shift lengths
When videos have different resolutions
answer: When some object categories appear far more frequently than others, potentially biasing the model

question: Why is it important to maintain consistent box tightness across an entire dataset?
options: Inconsistent tightness introduces label noise that can reduce model precision
It doesn't matter as long as the correct class is chosen
Only the color of the box matters
Loose boxes always train better models
answer: Inconsistent tightness introduces label noise that can reduce model precision

question: What should an annotator do when two different object classes overlap significantly in the same region?
options: Merge them into a single box
Draw separate boxes for each object per the guidelines, even if they overlap
Only label the larger object
Skip the frame entirely
answer: Draw separate boxes for each object per the guidelines, even if they overlap

question: What is 'anchor drift' when tracking a bounding box across frames?
options: Gradual, unintentional misalignment of the box from the object it should be tracking
The intentional movement of an object in the scene
A software feature to auto-correct boxes
The process of deleting a track
answer: Gradual, unintentional misalignment of the box from the object it should be tracking

question: Which situation most justifies creating a new track ID rather than continuing an existing one?
options: The object briefly went behind a pole for 2 frames
The object left the frame entirely and a different object of the same class enters later
The object changed lighting conditions slightly
The annotator got tired
answer: The object left the frame entirely and a different object of the same class enters later

question: In object detection labeling, what does 'truncation' refer to?
options: An object being partially cut off by the edge of the frame
An object being blurry
An object changing color
An object moving very fast
answer: An object being partially cut off by the edge of the frame

question: Why might guidelines specify a minimum bounding box size (e.g., ignore objects smaller than 10x10 pixels)?
options: To make the task pointless
Extremely small objects often provide little useful signal and are hard to label reliably
Small objects are always more important
There is no such practice in real annotation work
answer: Extremely small objects often provide little useful signal and are hard to label reliably

question: What is the risk of consistently drawing bounding boxes that are too loose (include excess background)?
options: The model may learn to associate background context as part of the object, reducing localization accuracy
It has no downstream effect
It speeds up model training with no drawbacks
It only affects video compression
answer: The model may learn to associate background context as part of the object, reducing localization accuracy

question: When a guideline says to label 'amodal' bounding boxes, what does that mean?
options: Boxing only the visible pixels of an object
Estimating and boxing the full extent of an object, including the occluded parts
Ignoring occluded objects completely
Using circles instead of boxes
answer: Estimating and boxing the full extent of an object, including the occluded parts

question: What is the purpose of a 'confidence score' sometimes requested alongside an annotation?
options: To indicate how certain the annotator is about the label's correctness
To indicate the annotator's typing speed
To rate the video quality
To determine the annotator's pay automatically in all cases
answer: To indicate how certain the annotator is about the label's correctness

question: Which of the following is the best practice when an object's class is genuinely ambiguous (e.g., could be a cat or a small dog)?
options: Pick randomly and move on
Use the guideline's specified fallback category or flag it for review as instructed
Always default to the most common class in the dataset
Leave it unlabeled with no explanation
answer: Use the guideline's specified fallback category or flag it for review as instructed

question: What does 'label leakage' mean in an annotation pipeline?
options: When annotators can see information (like model predictions or future frames) that biases their labeling in unintended ways
When a video file is leaked online
When too many labels are used in one project
When annotations are exported to the wrong file format
answer: When annotators can see information (like model predictions or future frames) that biases their labeling in unintended ways

question: Why do many annotation platforms show a pre-drawn AI-suggested bounding box for the annotator to adjust?
options: To speed up annotation via human-in-the-loop correction rather than drawing from scratch
Because annotators are not allowed to draw boxes themselves
To replace the need for human review entirely
Because AI suggestions are always perfectly accurate
answer: To speed up annotation via human-in-the-loop correction rather than drawing from scratch

question: If the AI-suggested bounding box is close but not perfectly aligned, what should the annotator do?
options: Accept it as-is to save time regardless of accuracy
Adjust it to be accurate according to the guidelines before submitting
Delete it and leave the frame blank
Report it as a bug and skip the frame
answer: Adjust it to be accurate according to the guidelines before submitting

question: What is 'over-annotation' and why is it a problem?
options: Labeling more objects or detail than the guidelines require, which wastes time and can introduce inconsistency
A required best practice in all tasks
Annotating too quickly
A term with no real meaning in this field
answer: Labeling more objects or detail than the guidelines require, which wastes time and can introduce inconsistency

question: A rubric states 'only label vehicles that are clearly in motion.' A car is parked but its brake lights are on. What should the annotator do?
options: Label it as in motion because the lights are on
Not label it as in motion, since a stationary car with lights on is not moving, unless guidelines say otherwise
Skip the entire frame
Label every vehicle in the frame regardless of motion
answer: Not label it as in motion, since a stationary car with lights on is not moving, unless guidelines say otherwise

question: What is the key difference between semantic segmentation and instance segmentation?
options: Semantic segmentation labels every pixel by class only; instance segmentation also distinguishes between individual objects of the same class
They are exactly the same
Instance segmentation only works on images, not video
Semantic segmentation uses bounding boxes only
answer: Semantic segmentation labels every pixel by class only; instance segmentation also distinguishes between individual objects of the same class

question: In polygon annotation, what is generally recommended when tracing an object's edge?
options: Use as few points as possible regardless of shape accuracy
Place vertices along the true contour of the object, adding more points at curves and fewer on straight edges
Always use exactly 4 points
Draw the polygon larger than the object for safety
answer: Place vertices along the true contour of the object, adding more points at curves and fewer on straight edges

question: What is a 'mask' in the context of segmentation annotation?
options: A pixel-level labeling that identifies which pixels belong to an object or class
A privacy filter applied to a video
A type of bounding box
A video compression technique
answer: A pixel-level labeling that identifies which pixels belong to an object or class

question: Why is polygon/segmentation annotation generally more time-consuming than bounding box annotation?
options: It requires tracing precise object boundaries rather than a simple rectangle
It requires no more effort than bounding boxes
Polygons are drawn automatically without human input
Segmentation tasks never involve real objects
answer: It requires tracing precise object boundaries rather than a simple rectangle

question: What does 'panoptic segmentation' combine?
options: Semantic segmentation and instance segmentation into one unified labeling task
Audio and video annotation
Bounding boxes and text labels only
Two different videos into one
answer: Semantic segmentation and instance segmentation into one unified labeling task

question: When segmenting a person holding a bag, how should the bag typically be handled?
options: Included as part of the person's mask always
Segmented as a separate object/class unless the guideline explicitly says to merge them
Ignored entirely
Merged with the background
answer: Segmented as a separate object/class unless the guideline explicitly says to merge them

question: What is a common cause of jagged or inaccurate segmentation masks?
options: Using too few polygon points around curved edges or working at low zoom
Using a mouse instead of a keyboard
Working too slowly
Using the correct class label
answer: Using too few polygon points around curved edges or working at low zoom

question: Why might an annotator be asked to zoom in before finalizing a segmentation mask?
options: To improve boundary precision along fine details like hair or fingers
Zooming has no effect on accuracy
To make the task take longer intentionally
Because the software requires it to save the file
answer: To improve boundary precision along fine details like hair or fingers

question: What should be done with holes in an object (e.g., the empty space inside a donut shape) during segmentation?
options: Always fill them in as part of the mask
Exclude the hole from the mask if the guideline defines the object by its solid, visible material only
Ignore the object entirely
Segment the hole as a separate full object
answer: Exclude the hole from the mask if the guideline defines the object by its solid, visible material only

question: What is 'keypoint annotation' most commonly used for?
options: Marking specific structural points on an object, such as human joints for pose estimation
Labeling the color of an object
Counting the total number of frames
Measuring video file size
answer: Marking specific structural points on an object, such as human joints for pose estimation

question: In human pose estimation, what should an annotator do if a joint (e.g., left elbow) is not visible in the frame?
options: Guess its location precisely with full confidence
Mark it according to guidelines, typically as 'not visible' or estimate it only if explicitly instructed to for occluded points
Delete the entire pose annotation
Always place it at the center of the frame
answer: Mark it according to guidelines, typically as 'not visible' or estimate it only if explicitly instructed to for occluded points

question: Why is the order/index of keypoints (e.g., point 1 = nose, point 2 = left shoulder) important?
options: It ensures the model receives consistent, correctly structured data across the whole dataset
It has no importance as long as points are placed somewhere on the body
It only matters for audio annotation
The order changes based on annotator preference
answer: It ensures the model receives consistent, correctly structured data across the whole dataset

question: What is 'skeletal tracking' in video annotation?
options: Tracking the connected set of keypoints (skeleton) of a subject across frames over time
Tracking only bones visible via X-ray footage
A method for annotating audio
A way to compress video files
answer: Tracking the connected set of keypoints (skeleton) of a subject across frames over time

question: When annotating facial landmarks, what is a common challenge specific to video (vs. still images)?
options: Maintaining consistent landmark placement as the face moves, rotates, or is partially occluded across frames
Facial landmarks are never used in video
There are no challenges specific to video
Faces never move in video
answer: Maintaining consistent landmark placement as the face moves, rotates, or is partially occluded across frames

question: What does a low-confidence or 'uncertain' flag on a keypoint typically indicate?
options: The annotator is unsure of the exact pixel location due to occlusion, blur, or ambiguity
The keypoint is definitely wrong
The video has no audio
The annotator has finished the task
answer: The annotator is unsure of the exact pixel location due to occlusion, blur, or ambiguity

question: What is the main goal of multi-object tracking (MOT) annotation?
options: Assigning and maintaining a consistent identity to each object as it moves across multiple frames
Labeling each frame independently with no connection between frames
Counting the total number of frames in the video
Removing objects from the video
answer: Assigning and maintaining a consistent identity to each object as it moves across multiple frames

question: What is an 'ID switch' error in object tracking?
options: When the tracker/annotation mistakenly assigns a different ID to the same object mid-track, or swaps IDs between two objects
When an annotator changes their username
When a video file is renamed
When the frame rate changes
answer: When the tracker/annotation mistakenly assigns a different ID to the same object mid-track, or swaps IDs between two objects

question: If two similar-looking objects (e.g., identical twin cars) cross paths and separate, what is the biggest risk?
options: An ID switch, where the tracker/annotator mixes up which object is which after the crossing
The video file becoming corrupted
The frame rate increasing
There is no risk in this scenario
answer: An ID switch, where the tracker/annotator mixes up which object is which after the crossing

question: What technique can help an annotator avoid ID switches when objects cross paths?
options: Carefully reviewing frames just before, during, and after the crossing to confirm identity using visual cues like clothing or trajectory
Always assigning a new ID after any crossing
Ignoring the crossing event entirely
Randomly picking an ID
answer: Carefully reviewing frames just before, during, and after the crossing to confirm identity using visual cues like clothing or trajectory

question: What does 'track fragmentation' mean?
options: A single object's track is incorrectly split into multiple disconnected track segments
The video is split into multiple files
The annotator's screen freezes
A bounding box is drawn multiple times in one frame
answer: A single object's track is incorrectly split into multiple disconnected track segments

question: Why might an annotation guideline require a minimum track duration (e.g., ignore tracks shorter than 3 frames)?
options: Very short tracks are often noise (e.g., detection flicker) and provide limited training value
Short tracks are always the most valuable
It is a rule with no real justification
To reduce the number of videos needed
answer: Very short tracks are often noise (e.g., detection flicker) and provide limited training value

question: In video tracking annotation, what is 'linear interpolation' typically used for?
options: Estimating intermediate bounding box positions between two manually annotated keyframes, assuming straight-line movement
Adjusting video color balance
Removing background noise from audio
Compressing the video file size
answer: Estimating intermediate bounding box positions between two manually annotated keyframes, assuming straight-line movement

question: Why should an annotator manually review and correct interpolated frames, rather than trusting them blindly?
options: Interpolation assumes linear motion, which can be inaccurate if the object changes speed, direction, or is occluded
Interpolated frames are always perfectly accurate
Manual review is never necessary
Interpolation only works for audio data
answer: Interpolation assumes linear motion, which can be inaccurate if the object changes speed, direction, or is occluded

question: What is the purpose of a 'trajectory' visualization in a tracking annotation tool?
options: To show the path an object has taken across frames, helping annotators spot errors or inconsistencies
To display the annotator's mouse movements
To show video file metadata
To indicate network latency
answer: To show the path an object has taken across frames, helping annotators spot errors or inconsistencies

question: A car exits the left side of the frame and, 2 seconds later, a visually similar car enters from the right side. Should they share the same track ID?
options: Yes, always, since they are the same class
No, generally not, unless there is strong evidence (trajectory, guideline rules) that it's the same physical object
Only if the annotator is unsure
Yes, because track IDs should never be reused
answer: No, generally not, unless there is strong evidence (trajectory, guideline rules) that it's the same physical object

question: What does 'MOTA' (Multiple Object Tracking Accuracy) broadly measure?
options: Overall tracking performance considering false positives, missed detections, and ID switches
The audio quality of a video
The annotator's typing speed
The resolution of the camera used
answer: Overall tracking performance considering false positives, missed detections, and ID switches

question: Why is smooth, jitter-free bounding box tracking important for downstream model training?
options: Jittery boxes introduce noisy motion signals that can confuse models learning object dynamics
Jitter has no effect on training
Smoothness only matters for human viewers, not models
Models cannot process bounding boxes at all
answer: Jittery boxes introduce noisy motion signals that can confuse models learning object dynamics

question: When a fast-moving object causes significant motion blur, what is the best annotation practice?
options: Skip the object entirely for the whole video
Annotate the object's best-estimated true extent per guidelines, noting blur if the platform supports a flag
Draw the box around the entire blurred trail with no consideration of guidelines
Always mark it as a different object class
answer: Annotate the object's best-estimated true extent per guidelines, noting blur if the platform supports a flag

question: What is the benefit of reviewing a tracked object's annotation in 'playback mode' rather than frame-by-frame only?
options: It helps catch flicker, jitter, or ID errors that are easier to see in motion than in static frames
Playback mode is purely cosmetic and has no analytical benefit
It replaces the need for any frame-by-frame review
It automatically fixes all errors
answer: It helps catch flicker, jitter, or ID errors that are easier to see in motion than in static frames

question: If guidelines state 'track vehicles only while at least 25% visible,' and a car becomes 80% occluded for 10 frames then reappears, what should happen to its track?
options: The track should end immediately and never resume
The track should pause/mark as occluded during those frames and resume with the same ID once visibility exceeds the threshold again
A new track ID must be created regardless of context
The entire video should be discarded
answer: The track should pause/mark as occluded during those frames and resume with the same ID once visibility exceeds the threshold again

question: What is 'temporal action localization'?
options: Identifying the exact start and end time of a specific action within a longer video
Locating an object's pixel coordinates in a single frame
Measuring video file size over time
Converting video to a different resolution
answer: Identifying the exact start and end time of a specific action within a longer video

question: If a guideline defines 'walking' as starting when a foot first leaves the ground, where should the start timestamp be placed?
options: At the very beginning of the video regardless of content
At the exact frame where the foot first lifts off the ground, per the definition given
At a random point during the walking motion
At the end of the walking action
answer: At the exact frame where the foot first lifts off the ground, per the definition given

question: What is a common challenge when labeling the boundary between two consecutive actions (e.g., 'sitting down' then 'standing up')?
options: There is never any ambiguity between actions
Precisely pinpointing the transition frame, which can be subjective without a clear operational definition
Actions never transition into each other
The video format prevents transition labeling
answer: Precisely pinpointing the transition frame, which can be subjective without a clear operational definition

question: Why do action recognition guidelines often include explicit, operational definitions (e.g., 'a wave requires at least 2 side-to-side hand motions')?
options: To reduce subjectivity and increase consistency across annotators
To make the task deliberately confusing
Definitions are unnecessary for action labeling
To increase annotation time without benefit
answer: To reduce subjectivity and increase consistency across annotators

question: How should overlapping actions be handled if a person is both 'talking' and 'walking' at the same time, and both are valid labels?
options: Only one label can ever be applied per guideline restrictions in all cases
Apply both labels with their respective time ranges if the guidelines allow multi-label/overlapping annotation
Ignore both actions since they overlap
Merge them into a new, undefined label
answer: Apply both labels with their respective time ranges if the guidelines allow multi-label/overlapping annotation

question: What is the purpose of labeling 'background' or 'no action' segments in an action recognition dataset?
options: To give the model negative examples so it learns to distinguish actions from non-action periods
Background segments are never labeled in any dataset
To increase the file size unnecessarily
To replace the need for positive action labels
answer: To give the model negative examples so it learns to distinguish actions from non-action periods

question: In event annotation, what does a 'pre-roll' or 'buffer' requirement (e.g., label 2 seconds before the event starts) typically help with?
options: Giving the model context leading up to the event, useful for prediction/early-detection tasks
Making the video file smaller
Removing the need for an end timestamp
It has no practical use
answer: Giving the model context leading up to the event, useful for prediction/early-detection tasks

question: Which is the most appropriate approach if an action happens too briefly to be clearly visible (e.g., 1-2 frames of motion blur)?
options: Always label it as a full-duration, clearly defined action
Follow the guideline's minimum-duration or ambiguous-event rule, which may mean flagging or excluding it
Ignore all guidelines and use personal judgment silently
Delete the video from the dataset without documentation
answer: Follow the guideline's minimum-duration or ambiguous-event rule, which may mean flagging or excluding it

question: What is 'inter-annotator agreement' (IAA)?
options: A measure of how consistently different annotators label the same data
The pay rate agreed upon between annotators and the company
A software tool for drawing bounding boxes
The number of annotators assigned to a project
answer: A measure of how consistently different annotators label the same data

question: What does Cohen's Kappa account for that raw percent agreement does not?
options: The rate of agreement expected to occur by chance
The speed of annotation
The resolution of the video
The number of classes only, with no statistical adjustment
answer: The rate of agreement expected to occur by chance

question: A Cohen's Kappa score of 0.85 generally indicates:
options: Poor agreement
Almost perfect / very high agreement between annotators
No agreement at all
That the task is impossible
answer: Almost perfect / very high agreement between annotators

question: What is the purpose of a 'consensus' or 'majority vote' pipeline in annotation projects?
options: To combine multiple annotators' labels on the same item to produce a more reliable final label
To let one annotator decide everything unilaterally
To remove the need for any guidelines
To slow down the project intentionally
answer: To combine multiple annotators' labels on the same item to produce a more reliable final label

question: Why might a project use 'triple annotation' (3 independent annotators per item) for critical tasks?
options: To increase reliability and catch errors via majority consensus, especially for high-stakes data
It is always required regardless of task importance
To reduce costs
To eliminate the need for guidelines
answer: To increase reliability and catch errors via majority consensus, especially for high-stakes data

question: What is a 'QA reviewer' or 'auditor' role in an annotation pipeline?
options: Someone who reviews completed annotations for accuracy and provides feedback or corrections
The person who writes the video content
A role that has no interaction with annotators
An automated bot with no human oversight
answer: Someone who reviews completed annotations for accuracy and provides feedback or corrections

question: If your QA rejection rate is unusually high compared to peers, what is the most constructive next step?
options: Ignore the feedback and continue as before
Review the specific rejected examples, re-read the guidelines, and ask clarifying questions about recurring mistakes
Immediately quit the project
Blame the QA reviewer without reviewing your own work
answer: Review the specific rejected examples, re-read the guidelines, and ask clarifying questions about recurring mistakes

question: What is a 'calibration session' in an annotation project?
options: A meeting where annotators review sample cases together to align their understanding of the guidelines before starting bulk work
A software update process
A one-on-one performance review only
A session to fix a broken annotation tool
answer: A meeting where annotators review sample cases together to align their understanding of the guidelines before starting bulk work

question: Why are 'edge cases' specifically valuable to discuss during calibration?
options: They tend to cause the most disagreement between annotators and reveal gaps in the guidelines
They are the easiest cases and need no discussion
Edge cases never occur in real datasets
They are only relevant to audio annotation
answer: They tend to cause the most disagreement between annotators and reveal gaps in the guidelines

question: What does it mean if guidelines are described as a 'living document'?
options: The guidelines may be updated over time as new edge cases and clarifications emerge
The guidelines are printed on paper only
The guidelines never change once published
The guidelines are generated randomly for each task
answer: The guidelines may be updated over time as new edge cases and clarifications emerge

question: What is the best response when you disagree with a QA correction that you believe is actually wrong?
options: Silently comply without ever raising concerns
Politely raise the specific disagreement with reference to the guideline, asking for clarification
Argue aggressively and refuse to make further corrections
Ignore all future QA feedback from that reviewer
answer: Politely raise the specific disagreement with reference to the guideline, asking for clarification

question: What is 'annotator drift' over the course of a long project?
options: A gradual, often unintentional shift in how an annotator applies labeling standards over time
The physical movement of an annotator's mouse cursor
A feature that automatically corrects annotations
A term with no meaning in this field
answer: A gradual, often unintentional shift in how an annotator applies labeling standards over time

question: Which practice helps prevent annotator drift on long projects?
options: Periodically re-reviewing guidelines and gold-standard examples throughout the project
Never reviewing your own past work
Working as fast as possible with no breaks
Avoiding all communication with QA or team leads
answer: Periodically re-reviewing guidelines and gold-standard examples throughout the project

question: What is a 'confusion matrix' used for in evaluating annotation or model accuracy?
